newsitem.title: KENYA: Limping Mandela in Kenya for "Great Lakes" summit.
newsitem.headline: Limping Mandela in Kenya for "Great Lakes" summit.

text.p: A limping Nelson Mandela joined eight other African leaders in Kenya on Monday for a summit on the crisis in central Africa's Great Lakes region.
The South African president, succumbing to international pressure to get involved, was taking part in high-level talks on the conflicts in Zaire and Burundi for the first time.
The summit opening was delayed and was unlikely to start before 4.30 p.m. (1330 GMT).
Zaire will not attend, Kenyan officials said.
Mandela, wearing one of his trademark patterned shirts, was limping heavily on arrival at Nairobi airport but walked unaided to review the Kenyan army honour guard.
He took the arm of his host, President Daniel arap Moi, before writing in the visitors' book in the VIP pavilion: "Visiting Kenya has fulfilled a life dream."
There was no immediate explanation for the limp from the South African delegation.
Mandela, on his first official visit to Kenya, joined the presidents of Eritrea, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe and Ethiopia's prime minister who all arrived before him.
The summit, which looked likely to stretch into Tuesday, will focus on the search for a ceasefire and political settlement in eastern Zaire.

Rebels there launched a well-planned offensive in mid-October and now control eastern key towns. They say their ultimate goal is to end the 31-year reign of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko who is due to return to Kinshasa on Tuesday.

The crisis in the Great Lakes -- an area roughly comprising Zaire, Burundi, Rwanda and parts of Tanzania and Uganda -- is potentially the most far-reaching in Africa since the Nigerian civil war in the late 1960s.
Zaire boycotted the first Nairobi summit on the Great Lakes last November 5, refusing to sit down with Rwanda which it accuses of sponsoring the rebellion.
Dashing Kenyan hopes that this second summit would see the start of some dialogue between Zaire and Rwanda, Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo of Zaire failed to turn up on Monday.
The rebels have not been invited to take part and nor has Burundi's military regime, Kenyan officials say.
An estimated 150,000 people have died since 1993 in ethnic war in Burundi between majority Hutus and minority Tutsis who dominate the armed forces.

The Zaire conflict has pushed Burundi into the background but U.N. human rights monitors say the level of killing has gone on unabated. Some of the leaders expected in Nairobi will argue for the lifting or easing of economic sanctions imposed on Burundi after Major Pierre Buyoya's military coup last July 25.

"Burundi is part of the Great Lakes region yet it has not been invited and we have severe problems and we think they should be discussed," Burundi's presidency spokesman, Jean-Luc Ndizeye, said on Monday.
"We have no idea what they will do about Burundi in the summit. I don't see why countries thousands of miles away are invited," he told Reuters by telephone from Bujumbura.

Last November's Nairobi summit called in vain for a ceasefire in eastern Zaire and the deployment of a neutral international force to assist 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees caught up in the fighting.
Plans for the force were formally shelved last weekend.
About half the refugees in Zaire returned home peacefully last November and the exact number remaining is disputed.
The second largest concentration of Rwandan Hutu refugees is in Tanzania and a majority of the 500,000 in camps there were flooding back home on Monday.
The Hutus left Rwanda in 1994 after many in their community committed a genocide against Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
